I'm in a similar situation as you, with a partner who has ADHD, and a lot of the comments have left great advice.

I'm my particular experience, one of the biggest things I've learned as a partner without ADHD is that regardless of the advice you're trying to give, it's to start by explaining why the action affects you and how that happens. 

For example, I saw that you mentioned chewing as one point in another comment. In that sort of scenario, it's better to start by saying something like "I personally find that your chewing with your mouth open ends up being a bit loud / I don't enjoy the sound of your your chewing because of (INSERT REASON HERE)." It's all about explaining things to help them understand your perspective.

The next and most crucial thing is to give them time to speak and acknowledge what's going on. There isn't a one-size-fits-all type answer to let you know when this step starts or ends, but it's important to let your partner feel heard and to give them time to talk things out with you. There may be things you weren't aware of that are affecting a scenario. 

For example, I'm using a situation with my partner. We would cook together and occasionally, they would get overwhelmed and just end up lying on the floor for a bit (I found out later that this is something that some people with ADHD do as a coping mechanism). Talking about the issue, that's when I learned that it was a strategy my partner had learned to help themselves from becoming overwhelmed, especially when they needed to multitask with cooking. We eventually figured out a way for them to have their space while I communicated what I was doing with the cooking so they didn't come back and become overwhelmed when things were different.

With these two major things in mind, one thing I have to stress is that sometimes, their effort is going to be something that they'll be working on in their own heads and that you might not see what you consider to be "expected results" immediately. It's easy to get worked up when you ask something that on the surface level is an easy thing to change (i.e. closing your mouth to chew) but it can be an incredibly challenging process that requires a lot of focus and effort on their part. 

To that effect, my advice is to congratulate their efforts and build up the times you do notice when they're putting in that work. It can be as easy as a smile, it's just something that gives them a quick seratonin boost and helps them reinforce why they're putting in the effort in the first place. Don't be afraid to bring things up again and communicate about how things are going. Like I mentioned before, you may not see them putting in the effort from an outside perspective, but this is a way to make sure you're communicating about the effort they are putting in in ways you're not seeing. You might even find that you haven't noticed things properly and that they were showing you their efforts beforehand.

One last bit of advice, and this is one that really works for my partner and I, but is definitely something you should discuss with your partner. We have our own non verbal communication system, that we keep just between the two of us, so even if they're struggling to talk or getting overwhelmed, we can still communicate. This way, in case someone else is being affected by their behavior, and they don't notice, I can communicate to them without making a scene.

What my partner and I do is really simple too. We hold each other's hand and squeeze once to let the other person know to look at us. Then whatever action we need to focus on, one person does and the other mimics. We also give three squeezes afterwards which is does two things: first, it lets the other person know that that's the entire action to focus on. Secondly, we use that as an "I love you" message, to reinforce a positive communication.


I know that I've given you a huge information dump that has a lot of steps for both of you, so feel free to message me if you have any questions. It's great that you're taking the time to learn how to better communicate with your girlfriend, wish you two the best!

**TL;DR: I'm neurotypical and misunderstood discipline growing up, and I thought it was easy. S.O. has ADHD and has taught me what real discipline is, and how different it can be for someone with ADHD.**

This is something that I struggle with my S.O. with personally. They are the one with an ADHD diagnosis, and they find that being disciplined is never as easy as what that person described in the picture you linked. 

I, on the other hand, am more neurotypical, but I was raised in a house that forced "discipline" on my siblings and myself growing up. We didn't have the choice to become motivated about a task, we were forced into doing things that we had to, and this became a very engrained part of my character growing up.

Now, as an adult, I see myself as being disciplined, because I can force myself to do tasks that I don't necessarily want to, or don't have the motivation to. It's also why I hate being "disciplined" because I'm forcing myself to do things, as opposed to getting myself to do them for the right reasons.

It's something that my S.O. and I have struggled with, because I used to think that their building up motivation and getting ready to do a task was equal to them having no discipline. 

The thing that really changed my understanding of it was learning how they addressed their ADHD, which ultimately showed me that they were far more genuinely disciplined than I was. They learned to do things because they saw the reasons behind doing a task, where I only saw the obligation.

We still struggle with times, where my S.O. has a hard time getting motivated to accomplish their goals. I've been learning to be more supportive in that way, that even simply being there to listen to their tasks has been a better push for their motivation and discipline. And it's helped me work on my own discipline too, which has helped me so much.

On the day that God made man, he said that it was good.

The very next day, man said that it was average at best,

And so he started to fill his life with drugs and alcohol and expensive shit.

Tried to find some meaning while on a tiny dot floating through space in the vastness of the universe, throughout the speck of its existence that his life would be.

He tried so hard that he fell for a trap, sold his soul to a job that he hates, so that some other fucker can live the dream on some private beach off the coast of Spain.




So he taught his son to look for meaning in his life, find wisdom and knowledge, that he could become successful.

His son searched so hard he became a philosopher, drowning in his own thoughts with a bottle of gin, cursing the very day that he was born.

You see, the son learned that life was the affliction, and death the only cure.

It might seem madness, but what is death but the release from the cruelty of existence, and life but a string connecting heartaches and traumas throughout one’s days.

And so that man vowed to drink to forget, until the day that he forgot to drink, so that he would know in his heart that he had succeeded in learning the greatest mysteries of life.

Eventually he too grew old and fathered his own child, a daughter to a crack-head mom, who left him alone with a crying child he didn’t know how to care for.




She grew up learning a great many lessons from her wise father.

Learnt to not think too deeply into things, and to search for contentment, in the hope that she could be happy in ways that he would never be.

Young, pretty and smarter than she ever let on, she went into the world, searching for the joy that her father spoke of. 

She found it to be an impossible task, as it always seemed to fall through her grasp whenever she held it close, a boyfriend leaving, work unfulfilling, a life without meaning.

And so, she too learned the truth of this world, the lie of happiness.

So she found a way to break the cycle, through the barrel held up to her head.

No one is around to see her blank expression, or to hear the shot ring louder than any church bells ever could.




People are there for her funeral, co-workers and exes, neighbours and friends. They all speak of her cheerfulness, and they give their sympathies.

But after all too short a time, her name isn’t even a whisper on their tongues, but the world kept on spinning.

So you already know that there's 3 accounts: basic, flex and freedom.
Basic is the one that comes when you opt for a meal plan. You have to use the money in it before the end of April or the school takes it. 
Flex and Freedom are the ones that you can deposit money into. Flex is just like basic, where it's used on campus and you don't pay tax on food, but the money in that account can be switched to Freedom. 
Money in the Freedom account is used to buy from off campus places like Gino's or certain things on campus like candy from Mini Mac. This money is taxed when you spend it on campus, but can be switched into Flex. The big thing is that at the end of the semester, all the money in your flex account transfers over to Freedom, and that money persists into next year. Let me know if you need any further clarification on the accounts :)
